correctness.rationale: Each unitary divisor selects whole prime-power blocks; hence sigma*(n)/n=product(1+1/p^a). The class containing n has sum at least n, so three equal classes require this ratio to be at least three. For at most five primes the ratio is at most that of the first five primes to exponent one: 6912/2310=1152/385<3, achieved at 2310. This includes n=1 by the empty product. Any six distinct primes have product at least 30030. For attainment, independently enumerating the subsets of (2,3,5,7,11,13) gave 64 different divisor products of total 96768. The two listed sets and their complement comprise 4, 5 and 55 different products of respective sums 32256 each. The infinite lower bound is analytic; the finite computation verifies the witness only.

evidence: The boundary multiplicity record states that in the squarefree pattern (1,1,1,1,1), I(n)<=I(2*3*5*7*11)=1152/385<3. Its larger classification is for ordinary divisors and Omega=5. The 2^a3^b5 and Mahanta–Saikia–Yaqubi results concern ordinary layeredness on restricted families.

The squarefree bound is nonetheless a direct match for the critical numerical obstruction, since changing the exponents to one only increases each factor of the unitary abundancy and gives ordinary abundancy on the radical.

originality.rationale: The figure is correct and the prior sources do not explicitly phrase it as an unrestricted unitary minimum. But the prior ordinary three-layered table already records the identical squarefree attainment case, and the prior boundary result gives the identical rational obstruction for squarefree five-prime support. The latter transfers to every n with at most five primes by the standard termwise comparison with its radical, independently of whether a partition lifts. Together with the primorial bound these imply the complete finding by a routine transfer. The explicit partition is a certificate of an already tabulated attainment case, not a new extremal result.
